Outcome: Routine screening should include quantitative analysis to detect large rearrangements (5.8% of cases) missed by standard PCR.

Study Title: MeCP2 mutations in children with and without the phenotype of Rett syndrome
Study type: Observational/Genotype-Phenotype Correlation Study
Clinical Evicdence reported: The study screened 116 patients. Mutations were found in 72% of classical Rett Syndrome cases and 33% (8 of 25) of atypical cases. It also reports rare cases of mutations in two males: one with Klinefelter’s syndrome and one with a unique Xq27-28 inversion.
Functional evidence: 30 different mutations were identified, including 17 novel mutations. Notable findings include a complex gene rearrangement involving the 3' UTR and the identification of skewed X-inactivation patterns in two asymptomatic carriers and six symptomatic girls.
Outcome observations: There is a significant correlation between mutation location and disease severity; mutations at the amino-terminus (start of the protein) lead to a more severe clinical presentation than those at the carboxyl-terminus (end of the protein). Clinical variability is driven by the specific mutation type, its position, and X-inactivation patterns.
Age of onset: Infantile (typically 6–18 months), followed by rapid regression.
Phenotype description: Classical Rett Syndrome featuring regression, hand stereotypies, and loss of speech.
EEG Findings: Characteristic epileptiform discharges and background slowing (common in MECP2-related Rett).
Severity: Mutation position-dependent, with amino-terminus mutations causing significantly more severe clinical presentation than carboxyl-terminus mutations.
Author classification: Pathogenic/Causative
Outcome: Mutations at the amino-terminus correlate with higher clinical severity; X-inactivation and mutation position drive clinical variability.
